objectives: Apply Einstein A + B coefficients + stimulated emission.
Reason about gain, threshold, + cavity stability.

slides.title: Stimulated emission + the basic laser
slides.body:
**LASER** = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

Einstein 1917: atoms emit light in three processes:
• **Spontaneous emission**: excited atom decays randomly, emits photon. Random direction + phase. Rate A_21.
• **Absorption**: photon absorbed; atom excited. Rate B_12 × ρ(ν).
• **Stimulated emission**: incoming photon triggers excited atom to emit identical photon (same direction, phase, frequency, polarization). Rate B_21 × ρ(ν).

Einstein coefficients related by: A_21 = (8πhν³/c³) B_21, B_12 = B_21 (for non-degenerate levels). Key: stimulated emission produces coherent identical photons → light amplification.

**Population inversion**: usually atoms are mostly in ground state; absorption dominates over emission. For lasing: need N_2 > N_1 (more excited than ground) → net amplification. Achieved by **pumping**.

**Pumping**:
- Optical (other laser, flashlamp, sun): excite atoms via absorption.
- Electrical: discharge (gas), p-n junction (diode), accelerated electron beam.
- Chemical: H₂ + F₂ → HF + light (chemical lasers).
- Gas-dynamic: rapid cooling of hot gas.

**3-level vs 4-level lasers**:
- 3-level (ruby): ground → upper → lower (= ground). Needs >50% population inversion (hard).
- 4-level (Nd:YAG, dye, most modern): ground → upper → metastable → terminal (≠ ground) → ground. Easier to invert.

**Threshold + saturation**: at low pump, no lasing (loss > gain). Above threshold, lasing starts; gain clamps to loss; population inversion saturates.

**Beam properties**:
- **Monochromatic**: narrow linewidth (cavity-mode + transition).
- **Coherent**: long coherence length (1 µm - 100 km depending on laser).
- **Directional**: narrow divergence (~mrad).
- **High intensity**: up to ~10²² W/m² focused (multi-petawatt lasers).

slides.title: Optical resonators + cavity stability
slides.body:
**Optical resonator** confines + amplifies light by trapping it between mirrors (Fabry-Perot cavity).

Longitudinal modes: standing waves with integer half-wavelengths between mirrors. Frequency spacing Δν = c/(2L) (free spectral range, FSR).

Transverse modes: TEM_00 (lowest order), TEM_01, TEM_10, etc. (Hermite-Gaussian for rectangular symmetry).

**Stability criterion** (g₁ g₂ stability, where g_i = 1 - L/R_i for mirror radii R_i):
- 0 ≤ g₁ g₂ ≤ 1: stable resonator (beams stay bounded after many round trips).
- Otherwise: unstable → energy escapes the resonator after few trips.
- Common stable configs: plano-concave (g₁=1, 0 < g₂ < 1), confocal (g₁ = g₂ = 0), concentric.
- Unstable resonators used for high-power: large mode volume + efficient power extraction.

**Q-factor**: ω × stored energy / power loss. High Q: long photon lifetime → narrow linewidth.
Line narrowing: Δν ~ FSR / F (F = finesse). High-F resonators (>10⁵) for spectroscopy + frequency standards.

**Mode selection**:
- Single-mode (single longitudinal): intracavity etalon, ring cavity.
- Single-transverse mode: aperture, lens-design.
- Multi-mode: cavity supports many; sum gives intensity fluctuations.

**Output coupler**: partially transmissive mirror that lets some light out. Reflectivity ~50-99% depending on gain + power. Higher R: lower threshold but lower output; lower R: higher threshold + higher extraction.

**Modern cavity designs**:
- Linear (Fabry-Perot): simple, common.
- Ring: traveling-wave; single-frequency operation; lower noise.
- Bow-tie: travels in figure-eight; common in OPOs.
- Cavity-enhanced spectroscopy: F ~ 10⁵; weak-signal detection.
- Whispering-gallery modes (WGM): microspheres + microtoroids; extremely high Q (~10¹⁰); narrow linewidth + nonlinear effects.

slides.title: CW, pulsed, + ultrafast lasers
slides.body:
**Continuous wave (CW)**: steady-state output. Stable + spectrally narrow. Examples: He-Ne, Ar-ion, semiconductor laser diode, fiber lasers (most operate CW).

**Pulsed lasers**: temporally modulated output for high peak power.

• **Free-running** flashlamp-pumped: pulse driven by pump duration (~ms).
• **Q-switched**: intracavity shutter holds energy then releases (~ns pulses, MW peak). Used: laser ranging, marking, surgery, machining. Driver: electro-optic (Pockels) or acousto-optic modulator.
• **Mode-locked**: phase-lock multiple longitudinal modes → ultrashort pulses. Repetition rate = c/2L (~80 MHz typical Ti:S laser). Pulse duration ~ inverse of bandwidth. Modern: <5 fs.
• **Chirped-pulse amplification (CPA)**: stretch pulse → amplify → compress. Avoids damage in gain medium. Mourou + Strickland 1985, Nobel 2018. Foundation of multi-PW ultrafast lasers.
• **Frequency combs**: precise comb of equally-spaced laser lines from mode-locked laser. Hänsch + Hall 2005 Nobel. Used for: optical frequency metrology, atomic clocks, astronomy + exoplanet RV searches.

**Notable laser systems**:
- **He-Ne** (632.8 nm, 1-50 mW): classroom + alignment.
- **Argon-ion** (488 + 514 nm): fluorescence microscopy, optical pumping. Mostly replaced by diodes.
- **Nd:YAG** (1064 nm, ns-CW): industrial, surgery. SHG → 532 nm (green pointer).
- **Ti:sapphire** (~800 nm, ultrashort 5fs-100fs): research workhorse.
- **Fiber laser** (1µm, 1.5µm): industrial cutting/welding (IPG, Coherent); telecom.
- **Excimer** (193, 248 nm): photolithography, eye surgery (LASIK).
- **CO₂** (10.6 µm, kW-CW): industrial cutting.
- **VCSEL + DFB diodes**: telecom, datacenter, lidar, mouse sensors.
- **Quantum cascade laser (QCL)**: mid-IR; spectroscopy.
- **Free-electron laser (FEL)**: tunable from THz to X-ray; massive facilities (LCLS, European XFEL).

**Recent advances**:
- **Petawatt + multi-petawatt** for relativistic plasma physics, attosecond pulses.
- **Frequency comb spectroscopy** + atomic clocks (10⁻¹⁸ precision).
- **Ultracold atom + optical lattice clocks**.
- **Optical phased arrays + integrated photonics** scaling lasers on chip.
- **High-power fiber lasers**: 100s kW single-mode for industrial.
- **Single-photon sources** for quantum networks.

question.question: Compute laser threshold + slope efficiency for a Nd:YAG laser
question.goal: A diode-pumped Nd:YAG laser has cavity round-trip loss 5%, output coupler T = 5%, gain medium absorbs 95% of pump. Pump-to-mode coupling efficiency 80%, photon-energy conversion (1064/808) = 0.76. Compute threshold + slope efficiency.

steps.reveal: Total loss = 5% (scattering, absorption, diffraction) + 5% (output coupler) = 10% round-trip.
g_th = 10% per round trip. Population inversion adjusts to provide this gain.

steps.prompt: Slope efficiency η_slope = η_pump × η_absorb × η_quantum × η_outcoupling?
steps.reveal: η_pump = 0.8 (coupling); η_absorb = 0.95 (gain medium); η_quantum = 0.76 (Stokes); η_out = T/(T+loss) = 0.05/0.10 = 0.5. Product = 0.8 × 0.95 × 0.76 × 0.5 = 0.289 = 28.9%.

steps.prompt: If pump threshold is 5 W + we pump 20 W: output power?
steps.reveal: P_out = 0.289 × (20 - 5) = 4.34 W at 1064 nm. Typical Nd:YAG diode-pumped efficiency. Higher T_OC raises slope but raises threshold; trade-off optimized per design + pump power.

question.question: Drag components to build a Michelson interferometer. Build it correctly: laser source → beam splitter → two mirrors (one fixed, one movable) → detector at the recombined output.
question.explanation: A **Michelson interferometer** uses a 50:50 beam splitter to divide a coherent laser beam into two arms, each terminated by an end mirror. Reflected beams recombine at the splitter; the recombined output goes to a detector. Difference in arm length Δd shifts interference fringes — used for: LIGO gravitational-wave detection (3-4 km arms, picometer sensitivity), Fourier-transform IR (FTIR) spectroscopy, surface profilometry, wavemeter, etc. **Key**: coherent source required (laser, not lamp); 50:50 beam-splitter (not absorber); identical-quality mirrors; one mirror movable (often PZT-driven) for scanning. Modern: Mach-Zehnder, Sagnac, Twyman-Green variants.

question.question: Why did the development of fiber lasers (1990s-2000s) revolutionize industrial materials processing?
options: Combined: high efficiency (~30% wall-plug), high beam quality (M² near 1 even at 100 kW for single-mode), excellent thermal management (long thin fiber distributes heat), reliable + maintenance-free vs flashlamp-pumped solid-state, fiber-deliverable to remote work-cell. Replaced CO₂ + DPSS for many cutting + welding + cladding applications. IPG Photonics dominant supplier; multi-billion industry. Drives faster + finer + cheaper laser materials processing globally.
question.explanation:
**Fiber-laser revolution** (~2000-2020):

*Pre-fiber-laser industrial lasers*:
- **CO₂ lasers**: 10.6 µm; high power; bulky + maintenance-heavy; mirror-based delivery only (no fiber at 10 µm). Dominant for cutting since 1970s.
- **Diode-pumped Nd:YAG (DPSS)**: 1064 nm; fiber-deliverable; lower efficiency (~10%); thermal-lensing limits power.
- **Lamp-pumped Nd:YAG**: legacy; even less efficient; high maintenance.

*Fiber-laser advantages*:

1. **Efficiency**: ~30% wall-plug efficiency (vs ~10% DPSS, ~5-10% CO₂). Direct diode pump into Yb-doped fiber.

2. **Beam quality**: long fiber acts as mode filter; output highly Gaussian (M² ≤ 1.3 typical, even at multi-kW). Critical for tight-focus cutting.

3. **Thermal management**: kilometer of thin fiber distributes heat over large surface area; no thermal-lensing in bulk crystal. Enables high CW power.

4. **Reliability**: fiber-spliced; no free-space alignment to drift; sealed; lifetime 100k+ hours.

5. **Compactness**: gain medium is the fiber; pump diodes + folded beam path → benchtop sizes for kW-class.

6. **Fiber delivery**: output fiber routes laser to workpiece; flexible robot integration; no fragile mirrors over the production line.

7. **Pulsed regimes**: easy to add modulators for pulsed/Q-switched operation; ns, ps, fs available.

*Power evolution*:
- 2000: ~100 W single-mode fiber laser.
- 2010: 10 kW multimode.
- 2020: 100 kW single-mode; multi-MW R&D.
- Today: routine 6-12 kW single-mode for cutting + welding.

*Industrial impact*:

- **Sheet-metal cutting**: 6 kW fiber laser replaced CO₂ for stainless + aluminum cutting; faster + finer + cheaper.
- **Welding**: deep-penetration keyhole welding at 5-20 kW; auto + battery industries.
- **3D printing (LPBF/SLM)**: powder-bed fusion with kW fiber lasers; medical + aerospace.
- **Marking + engraving**: 20-100 W pulsed fiber for industrial markers; replaced YAG.
- **Cladding + heat treatment**: surface treatment + repair.
- **Cleaning + rust removal**: pulsed fiber lasers for paint + oxide removal.

*Market dominance*:
- IPG Photonics (US/Russia origin): pioneered + dominated; market cap $1B-$10B.
- Trumpf, Coherent (II-VI), Han's Laser, Maxphotonics: major players.
- China + Europe + US compete; Chinese cutting market grew rapidly 2015-2024.

*Trade-offs*:
- CO₂ still preferred for: thick metal, certain plastics, glass cutting (10.6µm absorbs).
- DPSS for: short-pulse precision (fs/ps systems often crystal-based for power scaling).
- Diode lasers for: kW direct, simpler systems (~50% efficiency, M²~10-50).

*Future*:
- Higher power (multi-MW + research).
- Beam-shape engineering (e.g., ring intensity, vortex).
- Coherent + spectral beam combining of multiple fibers.
- Integration with sensing + AI for adaptive processing.

Fiber laser is a model of materials-science + photonics-engineering co-evolution paying off in industrial applications.

slides.workedSolution: Fiber lasers: ~30% wall-plug efficiency (vs ~10% DPSS / ~5-10% CO₂); high beam quality (M²~1.3 even at multi-kW); long fiber distributes heat; reliable maintenance-free operation; flexible fiber-routed delivery; pulsed variants available. Replaced CO₂ + DPSS for sheet-metal cutting, welding, 3D-printing, marking, cleaning. Power evolved 100W → 100kW single-mode 2000-2020. IPG Photonics + Trumpf + Coherent dominate; multi-billion industry. CO₂ still preferred for thick metal/glass.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the trio of CW, Q-switched, + mode-locked lasers + when each is used.
question.rubric: Mentions: CW = continuous, narrow-linewidth, steady; used for spectroscopy, fiber comm, alignment, basic cutting/welding. Q-switched = nanosecond pulses with high peak power; built by intracavity modulator that holds + releases. Used for: marking + drilling + ranging + surgery + tattoo removal + nonlinear conversion (SHG). Mode-locked = phase-locked longitudinal modes producing ultrashort pulses (ps, fs, even attoseconds with HHG). Repetition rate = c/2L (~80 MHz). Used for: time-resolved spectroscopy (femtochemistry), materials machining with cold ablation, multiphoton microscopy, frequency-comb metrology, attosecond science. CPA (chirped-pulse amplification, Mourou-Strickland Nobel 2018) extends to petawatt regimes for laser fusion + relativistic plasma physics. Concludes: pulse regime selected per peak/average power needs + temporal resolution requirements.
